vignette: Leo Tui was fifty-one years old when he sat in the clinic waiting room, still pressing his thumb against the left side of his ribs where the steering wheel had driven him hard during the collision. He had come to believe that the afternoon sun had blinded him just enough to miss the silver sedan swerving into his lane. When the metal shrieked and the airbag bloomed, the force pinned his chest and shoulders against the wheel, and a sharp, familiar pain shot through his left hip and ribs. What he remembered most clearly was not the impact itself, but the thick, sour smell of spilled whiskey and cheap perfume that hung in the crumpled hood where the other driver stood, unsteadily breathing out words Leo could barely hear. The other driver had been leaving a roadside pub, and the alcohol scent clung to the torn fabric of Leo's own door panel long after the tow truck arrived. A PCL5 score of fifty-two quantified a mind and body that had settled into a steady state of vigilance, though the numbers only partially captured the way his shoulders would suddenly lock when a vehicle crossed his line of sight. In the months that followed, Leo found himself turning his head at the sound of tires crunching on gravel, at the low rumble of engines idling at intersections, at the sudden clatter of car doors shutting. He had come to expect another strike at any moment, so when he noticed a delivery truck hitting a concrete loading dock two streets from his fabrication yard, he would stop mid-step. The sight of that dented metal, the flash of crumpled bumpers, pulled his attention inward until his own torso tightened, as though his body had never truly left the driver's seat. When the memory of the crash returned to him, it did not arrive as a simple thought. His ribs ached in the exact spots they had ached against the steering wheel, and his whole posture felt rigid, mirroring the position he had held in the wrecked cab. On quiet afternoons in the shop, when a service vehicle backfired near the bay door, the memory would rush back in a single wave: the smell of industrial solvent mingling with the ghost of that whiskey, the sound of grinding gears, the flash of crumpled steel, and the familiar pressure against his chest, until everything felt completely real across all his senses at once. His work as a welder in a coastal metal fabrication yard meant he spent his days amid heat, sparks, and the steady percussion of grinders and compressors. He had adjusted to the noise of the yard, but the proximity of the service road meant that the distant hum of highway traffic and the occasional screech of brakes never fully faded. Over the weeks, he began lingering longer by the side gate, watching the line of cars snake past before stepping out to load his tools. He avoided the main thoroughfare when the wind carried the smell of liquor from the truck stop across the lot, finding himself holding his breath until he passed the source. His wife, Maria, noticed how he would sit on the porch in the evenings, his legs drawn up and his weight resting on his left leg, perfectly still, as though bracing for another impact. What frightened him most was not the idea of driving again, but the certainty that his body would remain locked in that same rigid posture while the world continued moving, the alcohol tang and the car sounds settling around him without disturbing the quiet. He had come to believe that the steel he shaped daily was safe, predictable, and grounded, unlike the glass and rubber machines that rushed past on the road. Yet the memories returned without warning, and each time his ribs tightened and his hip throbbed, the sensation settled over him like a heavy apron. When a neighbor's car alarm echoed through the neighborhood late one November night, Leo sat up in bed, his hands gripping the mattress, his breath shallow, the familiar alcohol scent of a passing food truck drifting through the screen door. What he had avoided most in recent months was not the road itself, but the unbroken certainty that his body was still caught in that collision, waiting for the next strike. He had finally made the appointment when he realized he could no longer tolerate the quiet dread of listening to the highway from his own kitchen, and he had come to the clinic hoping to find a way to let his shoulders drop and his hips settle, to step outside and feel the air without waiting for the metal to groan.
